awd_titl_txt: Student Travel for Powder Metallurgy & Particulate Materials and Additive Manufacturing with Powder Metallurgy Conference (PowderMet & AMPM 2025); Phoenix, Arizona; 15-18 June 2025
awd_abstract_narration:
Powder metallurgy is widely applied in the manufacturing economy, directly impacting economic welfare and national security. This award supports student participation in the International Conference on Powder Metallurgy and Particulate Materials (PowderMet2025) and the co-located Additive Manufacturing with Powder Metallurgy (AMPM2025) conference, to be held 15-18 June 2025, in Phoenix, Arizona. The support provides an opportunity for outstanding student researchers to attend the advanced manufacturing conferences, present their work, learn from leading experts in the field, and interact with students from other institutions, fostering a sense of worldwide community of scientific inquiry. The supported students will present research posters and participate in the conference poster award competition, among other activities. The relationships with conference participants will help the students in determining their specific areas of interest in this broad field and create colleagues for future interactions and potential collaboration. This will not only stimulate learning and training for the students, but also allow them to be exposed to new research concepts in powder metallurgy and additive manufacturing.

The objectives of the student participation in PowderMet2025 and AMPM2025 are to (1) expand career-enhancing learning opportunities for a broader knowledge of powder metallurgy and metal additive manufacturing, (2) promote technology transfer and provide a forum to introduce new research and development activities, (3) promote collaborative partnerships between organizations in advanced manufacturing and in emerging technologies to increase workforce development, and (4) develop a workforce aligned with regional economies based on emerging technologies across the Nation. The conference organizers will support up to 35 successful student applicants, who study at US institutions. An emphasis will be placed on students who would otherwise not be able to attend the conference and students presenting their research results at the conference. The organizers will invite applications through conference announcements and other means. The awards will provide support toward registration and accommodation. The availability of this support will encourage the participation of graduate and undergraduate students who otherwise would be unable to afford attending highly specialized advanced manufacturing conferences.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This award supported student participation in PowderMet & AMPM 2025, held in Phoenix, Arizona, from June 15-18, 2025. PowderMet is a major conference for powder metallurgy and particulate materials, and AMPM focuses on additive manufacturing using metal powders. Together, the conferences bring together university researchers, students, engineers, manufacturers, equipment suppliers, and professional societies working in advanced manufacturing. The purpose of this award was to reduce financial barriers for student researchers from U.S. institutions so they could attend the conference, present their work, learn from current research and industrial practice, and build professional networks.
NSF support was used for 35 student attendees from U.S. universities. By helping cover core participation costs, the award made it possible for students to engage fully in the technical program rather than limiting participation because of financial constraints. The attending student group included undergraduate, master's, and Ph.D. students in fields such as materials engineering, mechanical engineering, manufacturing, industrial engineering, mechatronics, and biomedical engineering. This range of backgrounds helped expose students from multiple disciplines to powder metallurgy, particulate materials, and metal additive manufacturing.
The intellectual merit of the project came from placing students directly in a high-level technical environment where they could connect their own research to the broader field. Student participants prepared research posters and gave concise oral presentations through the student research programming. Their work addressed topics related to powder metallurgy, metal additive manufacturing, materials processing, microstructure-property relationships, mechanical behavior, and related manufacturing technologies. Students also attended technical sessions and learned about current challenges in powder production, compaction, sintering, metal injection molding, materials design, testing, and industrial applications.
The broader impacts of the award were centered on workforce development, professional access, and student retention in advanced manufacturing fields. Many students had limited previous exposure to the full scale of the powder metallurgy industry. Through the conference, they interacted directly with industrial exhibitors, academic researchers, government and laboratory participants, and professional society leaders. These interactions helped students better understand career paths in sectors such as aerospace, automotive, energy, medical devices, and defense. The experience also helped students see how their academic research connects to real manufacturing needs.
A key outcome was the mentorship provided to student grant recipients. Students were connected with mentors from MPIF, APMI, technical boards, and industry volunteers. Mentors helped students prepare for the conference, navigate the technical program, make professional introductions, and reflect on career opportunities. Student feedback highlighted the value of networking with companies and industry experts, the usefulness of mentor support, and the impact of seeing award-winning powder metallurgy designs and real-world manufacturing examples. This support turned a short conference visit into practical training in communication, collaboration, and career planning.
The award also helped disseminate student research beyond individual laboratories. Student posters were displayed at the conference, selected posters were posted publicly by MPIF, and eligible student work could be included through the conference proceedings process. Overall, the award strengthened the connection between university research and the powder metallurgy/additive manufacturing community while helping prepare the next generation of engineers and scientists for careers in U.S. advanced manufacturing.
